title: Junípero Serra, honestly
hook: founder of the California missions, canonized in 2015 amid pain for Indigenous communities

segments.voice: Yesterday, Louis de Montfort, the wandering preacher of Totus tuus, all yours. Your line was to Jesus through Mary. Today, a harder story, told honestly.

A bronze friar lies on the grass of a California park. Protesters have pulled him off his base with ropes. In recent years, more than one statue of this man has come down. Yet Pope Francis declared him a saint, at a Mass in the United States. A saint to some Catholics. To some Native Californians, the face of what happened to their ancestors. Both are true at once, and this story doesn't let anyone pick just one. The friar is Junípero Serra.
screen: `A STATUE PULLED DOWN.` → `A SAINT DECLARED.` → `BOTH ARE TRUE.`

segments.voice: First, the friar. Junípero Serra was a Franciscan from the island of Majorca. As a friar he took the name of Brother Juniper, a companion of Saint Francis. A teacher of theology, he left it all to preach in New Spain. Tradition says he walked huge distances on an injured leg. He went north with Spanish soldiers and settlers and helped found a chain of missions along the California coast. Second, what Catholics honor: his zeal, his endurance, his poverty. When soldiers abused Native people near the missions, he traveled to Mexico City and asked the viceroy for rules to restrain them. At the canonization, Pope Francis praised him as a defender of the dignity of the native community. Third, what Native voices remember. The missions were part of Spain's colonial project. Baptized Native people were not free to leave. They were made to work, and could be whipped as punishment, something Serra himself defended in writing. Disease spread through the mission communities, and languages, ceremonies and ways of life were broken. For their descendants, this isn't old history. It's family history. Pope Francis has also asked forgiveness for crimes committed against native peoples in the conquest of the Americas. Fourth, listening. The letter of James, in the Douay-Rheims, says: "let every man be swift to hear, but slow to speak, and slow to anger." Telling Serra's story honestly means letting the people who carry the wound speak first. Some Catholics honor him. Some Native Catholics grieve his canonization. Both are inside the Church, and both deserve to be heard.
screen: `A FRIAR FROM MAJORCA.` · `WHAT CATHOLICS HONOR.` · `WHAT NATIVE FAMILIES REMEMBER.` · `SWIFT TO HEAR, SLOW TO SPEAK.` · then, large: `LET EVERY MAN BE SWIFT TO HEAR.`

segments.voice: Choose one Indigenous voice to listen to, a book, a recorded talk, a song, a Native Catholic writing about the missions, and decide which one. Then picture hearing something that stings, notice the reply that rises in you, and let it sit, without arguing or explaining. If you pray, hold Indigenous Catholics, and every family still carrying this history, before God.
Junípero Serra. The Franciscan who helped found the California missions, honored as a saint by the Church and remembered with pain by Native families.
Your line: listen first. Swift to hear comes before slow to speak. That's day eight hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: The Church keeps Saint Junípero Serra's memorial in its calendar, and in California some dioceses and parishes pair it with listening sessions, prayer and work alongside Native communities, whose members hold a range of views on his sainthood.

fork.setup: you're Serra. soldiers near the missions are abusing Native people. what do you do?
options: keep quiet, since the missions depend on the soldiers.
travel to Mexico City and ask the viceroy to restrain them.
close the missions and sail home.
fork.reveal: he made the journey and asked for rules to rein in the soldiers. historians add that he also defended the friars' power to punish converts. both belong to his story.

original.note: Spanish: Juniper, the name he took as a friar, after Brother Juniper, a companion of Saint Francis.

chat.says: Why are people still arguing about Junípero Serra, if he's a saint?
options: Catholics honor his zeal, but the missions also meant forced labor, whipping and disease.
Some say he was never canonized at all, only beatified by an earlier pope.
Most of the anger is about the statues, not about anything he actually did.
chat.meaning: The lesson holds both: Serra's zeal and care, and the missions' forced labor, punishment and disease. Both voices are inside the Church.
